title: The three gunas on your plate
hookLine: Arjuna asks Krishna about faith, and the answer arrives as three kinds of food
carry: the three gunas show up on your plate
tomorrow: Let the guest be a god

lines: WHAT ABOUT FAITH WITHOUT THE RULES?
A PERSON IS MADE OF THEIR FAITH.
EVEN FOOD COMES IN THREE KINDS.
cards: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, deep into the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna a sharp question. What about people who worship with real faith, but set aside the rules in the books? Where do they stand?
Krishna's answer goes somewhere unexpected. Faith comes in three kinds, he says, and a person is made of their faith: as someone's faith is, so they are.
Then, to show how deep that runs, he turns to something everyone does every day. Even the food people love, he says, comes in three kinds.

teach.h: THE THREE GUNAS: CLARITY, RESTLESSNESS, HEAVINESS
teach.b: The three kinds follow the three gunas, one of Hinduism's big ideas: three qualities running through all of nature, and through every person. Sattva, clarity. Rajas, restlessness.
Sattvic food, paraphrased, increases life, vigor, strength, health, happiness and contentment: savory, smooth, nourishing, pleasing to the heart.

teach.h: TOO HOT, TOO SHARP, PAIN AFTER
teach.b: Rajasic food is too bitter, too sour, too salty, too hot, too sharp, too dry, burning, and the verse says it brings pain, grief and sickness. Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, gone off, left over, unclean.
Notice how Krishna sorts them: by effects. Sattvic food is defined by what it gives, rajasic food by what it leaves behind. The test is the hour after.
And the second list is full of too: hot and sour aren't banned, it's the excess that tips a meal into restlessness. Now put it beside Arjuna's question.
A person is made of their faith, and the food a person loves comes in the same three kinds. So the plate isn't separate from the spiritual life; it's part of it.
Every meal leans a little toward clarity, restlessness or heaviness, and so does the one eating it.

teach.h: A SATTVIC KITCHEN ON HOLY DAYS
teach.b: That's why many Hindu families keep a sattvic kitchen on holy days and fasts: simple, fresh food, and in many homes no onion or garlic, a custom drawn from later teaching rather than from these verses.
And it turns the question around. Not only, what should I eat. Also, what does what I reach for say about who I'm becoming?

how: Hindus who draw on the Bhagavad Gita speak of food as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, after the three gunas in its chapter seventeen; many families keep a sattvic kitchen on holy days and fasts, some avoiding onion and garlic, and offer food before eating.

food sorted by what it does to you, during and after
food sorted by price, from the plainest to the finest

they describe food by its qualities and by what it does to the one who eats it.
in the Gita, even the food people love comes in three kinds
chapter seventeen opens the food verses by sorting the food dear to each person into three kinds.

o: food that leans toward sattva, clarity, judged by what it does to the one who eats it.
a fixed list of dishes from one region of India, the same in every home.
any food at all, once a priest has blessed it.
games.why: the Gita sorts food by the three gunas and by its effects: sattvic food increases life and strength, rajasic food brings pain after, tamasic food is stale. holy-day kitchens lean toward the first.

practice: Bring to mind what you ate most recently, and the hour after it: light and clear, restless and a little wired, or heavy and dull. No score; just notice which guna it leaned toward.

Then picture your next plate, and before the first bite, offer it first, the way many Hindu families do, with a short prayer or a silent thanks. If you don't pray, simply look at the food for one full breath before you eat.

wordCard.voice: Food as practice. The Gita's three kinds of food, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, following the three gunas, sorted by what they do to the eater. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sattvika, of sattva, the quality of clarity. The Gita's first kind of food (17.8).

carryVoice: Your line: the three gunas show up on your plate. Krishna's test is the hour after. See you tomorrow.
